fields.foundation: The Ayyubid Empire was built by one man, Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, known in the West as Saladin. He was a Kurdish commander of exceptional political intelligence who began as a constrained vizier in Cairo and became the master of the largest Muslim realm between the Nile and the Tigris. Saladin's path to power began in March 1169, when his uncle Shirkuh, the Zengid general who had taken control of Fatimid Egypt, died suddenly and Saladin was appointed vizier in his place. Two years later, as the last Fatimid caliph al-Adid lay dying in September 1171, Saladin had the Friday sermon pronounced in the name of the Abbasid caliph of Baghdad. This ended the Shi'a Fatimid Caliphate and returned Egypt to Sunni allegiance, and the Ayyubid state dates from this moment. At first Saladin was held back by his nominal subordination to the Zengid ruler Nur al-Din in Damascus, but Nur al-Din's death in May 1174 freed him to expand on his own account. He took Damascus that autumn and absorbed the Zengid principalities of Syria and northern Mesopotamia one after another, by military pressure and by diplomacy. He sent his brother Turanshah to conquer Yemen in 1174, which secured the Red Sea route, took Aleppo in 1183 and received the submission of Mosul in 1186. The purpose of this long consolidation was explicit: Saladin was encircling the Crusader states of the Levant before delivering the decisive blow. The cause he fought for was jihad, above all the recovery of Jerusalem from Christian rule, and it gave his empire a purpose and a legitimacy that did not depend on the Kurdish origins of his family.
fields.socioeconomy: The Ayyubid Empire governed the most economically productive region of the medieval Middle East. It held Egypt, sustained by the annual Nile flood, and the commercial centres of Syria, the Levantine coast and Upper Mesopotamia. Egypt's agricultural surplus came from the fertile Nile Delta and the irrigation networks of the Nile valley. It financed Saladin's campaigns and the court culture of the Ayyubid sultans, and was distributed to commanders through the iqta system of revenue assignments. Egyptian commerce developed significantly in the period. The Cairo Citadel, begun by Saladin in 1176 and expanded by his successors, was the seat of government and a sign of the dynasty's spending on the city. Among the sultans al-Kamil in particular promoted trade with the Italian maritime republics: Venice, Pisa and Genoa secured commercial privileges in Alexandria and brought European goods into Egypt in exchange for spices, alum, sugar and textiles. The Syria-Palestine corridor was one of the busiest trading regions of the medieval world, connecting the overland routes from Iraq, Persia and Central Asia to the Mediterranean ports of Acre, Beirut and Tyre. Ayyubid rulers tolerated Crusader enclaves on the coast, an arrangement formalised in successive truces from the Treaty of Jaffa (1192) onward. This was partly a commercial calculation, because the Frankish ports channelled Mediterranean trade on which Muslim merchants also depended. The empire's economic weakness was its division into semi-autonomous principalities. Revenues were split among competing princes, and the resources for sustained campaigns against either the Crusaders or the Mongols could not be gathered.
fields.military: The Ayyubid army was built on the Kurdish and Turkic warrior traditions of Saladin's milieu. Its core was a professional cavalry of mamluks, slave soldiers mostly of Turkic origin, supplemented by Kurdish and Turkmen contingents, Arab auxiliaries and the forces of subordinate princes. Saladin's gift lay less in tactics than in strategy and psychology. He understood that the Crusader states could only be defeated by a unified Muslim army that denied them the chance to exploit divisions among their neighbours, and he consolidated Egypt, Syria and Mesopotamia patiently in order to create that force. The strategy reached its end at the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187. Saladin drew the Crusader army out from the springs of Sephoria into waterless terrain at the height of summer and denied it access to the Sea of Galilee, so that the entire field army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem had to fight under extreme disadvantage. The victory was total: the army was destroyed, the relic of the True Cross captured and King Guy of Lusignan taken prisoner. Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187. The Third Crusade (1189–1192) showed the limits of Ayyubid power against determined European opponents. Saladin lost Acre to the combined forces of Richard I of England and Philip II of France in 1191 and was defeated in the field at Arsuf, though he retained Jerusalem under the Treaty of Jaffa. Later Ayyubid armies performed worse. Sultans spent their resources suppressing the ambitions of rival Ayyubid princes more than confronting external enemies. They also relied more and more on mamluk regiments, above all al-Salih Ayyub's Bahriyya, and so created a professional military establishment that proved more durable and cohesive than the dynasty it served.
fields.governance: Saladin distributed the empire's territories as appanages among his kinsmen, and Ayyubid government was pulled between that decision and the practical requirements of centralised rule. His reasoning was practical. By giving his brothers, sons and nephews direct control of Egypt, Damascus, Aleppo, Yemen and the Jazira, he secured their loyalty and their military contribution to the jihad while retaining supremacy as sultan. The result was a decentralised family confederation, often described as semi-feudal, in which each prince maintained his own court, army and revenues while acknowledging the senior sultan's authority. Egypt, the economic heartland, was usually the senior ruler's direct domain and the principal source of the resources that sustained central authority. The Cairo Citadel was built on a spur of the Muqattam Hills overlooking the city and continuously developed by Saladin's successors. It became the administrative centre of Ayyubid Egypt and is among the most impressive monuments of medieval Islamic rule to survive. The Ayyubid sultans patronised religious scholarship, endowed madrasas that consolidated Sunni learning in former Fatimid Egypt, and restored the Dome of the Rock and the al-Aqsa Mosque to Muslim worship after the reconquest of Jerusalem. Shafi'i jurisprudence predominated at the Ayyubid court, though the dynasty also endowed institutions for the other Sunni schools. The sultans cultivated the religious legitimacy they needed as defenders of Islam and protectors of the holy places. The critical failure was the absence of any accepted mechanism of succession. There was no rule of primogeniture, and the death of a senior sultan repeatedly set his heirs fighting, which drained the dynasty's military and financial resources.
fields.impact: The Ayyubid Empire is remembered chiefly for Saladin. His reconquest of Jerusalem in 1187 was followed by relatively merciful treatment of its Christian inhabitants, in sharp contrast to the massacre that accompanied the First Crusade's capture of the city in 1099, and from this grew one of the medieval world's longest-lived legends of noble warfare. Saladin's reputation crossed religious boundaries. Christian writers celebrated him as a model of chivalric virtue even though he had taken Jerusalem from them, and his exchanges of courtesies with Richard I during the Third Crusade passed into Western literary tradition. The Ayyubid reconquest permanently changed the political geography of the Levant. The Crusader coastal states that survived the Third Crusade lasted another century but never again threatened Muslim dominance of the interior, and the balance of power established after Hattin set the course that led to the fall of Acre in 1291. The dynasty founded madrasas across Egypt and Syria, and this patronage strengthened the institutions of Sunni learning in the region. The Ayyubid period also saw significant intellectual and artistic production, particularly in Cairo, Damascus and Aleppo, where the Citadel was rebuilt in its present form. The dynasty's greatest unintended legacy was the Mamluk Sultanate that replaced it. The slave-soldier system on which the later Ayyubids relied produced an institution of exceptional military effectiveness. It defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260, the first decisive check to Mongol expansion in the Middle East, and governed Egypt and Syria until the Ottoman conquest of 1517.
fields.decline: The Ayyubid Empire's decline began with the decisions Saladin made during his rise. He settled the empire's territories as autonomous principalities on his sons, brothers and nephews, above all in the arrangements of 1186. This secured the loyalty needed to win at Hattin and recover Jerusalem, but it ensured that his death would start a dynastic struggle capable of undoing much of what he had spent nearly two decades building. The succession conflict that broke out soon after Saladin's death in March 1193 was the first of many. His sons al-Afdal and al-Aziz fought over Damascus and Egypt, and only the patient statesmanship of Saladin's brother al-Adil allowed the realm to be reunited under his authority by 1200. Al-Adil's capable reign (1200–1218) and that of his son al-Kamil (1218–1238) showed that a strong sultan could hold the Ayyubid lands together, but each succession brought renewed conflict. Al-Kamil ceded Jerusalem to the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II by diplomacy in the Treaty of Jaffa (1229). He gave up the city whose recovery had defined Saladin's reign in return for support against his own Ayyubid relatives. This was the ideological low point of the dynasty and showed how far the founding ideal of jihad had been subordinated to dynastic survival. Egypt was lost to the Mamluks in 1250, after Sultan Turanshah was murdered by his father's own Bahri mamluks, and with it went the economic foundation of the entire system. The Mongol invasion of the Levant in 1259–1260, which followed the destruction of Baghdad in 1258, sacked Aleppo and ended the principalities of Aleppo and Damascus under al-Nasir Yusuf. It extinguished most of what remained, although Hama survived as a Mamluk vassal into the fourteenth century. The Battle of Ain Jalut was fought and won by the Mamluks, not the Ayyubids. Of the two products of the dynasty's military system, the Mamluk institution had proved the more durable.
fields.summary: The Ayyubid Empire was short-lived. Saladin united Egypt and Syria against the Crusaders, and the dynasty was then displaced by the very mamluk soldiers its later sultans had relied upon. The state rested on the ability of a single founder and on the generous distribution of power among his kinsmen, and those same kinsmen undid it once the founder was gone.
fields.teaser: Saladin's Ayyubid dynasty recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187 and changed the balance of power in the medieval Middle East. Saladin himself became a revered hero in both Islamic and European memory.
fields.t0: Founded by the Kurdish commander Saladin, it united Egypt, Syria and Upper Mesopotamia against the Crusader states.
fields.t1: Saladin's victory at Hattin and recapture of Jerusalem in 1187 permanently shifted the balance in the Levant.
fields.t2: Divided among quarrelling kinsmen, it was overthrown by its own mamluk soldiers in 1250 and finished by the Mongols.
fields.dyk: Saladin's nephew, Sultan al-Kamil, later handed Jerusalem to Emperor Frederick II by treaty in 1229, in return for help against his own Ayyubid relatives.
